edges.effect_quant: In 490 adults from TILDA, GrimAge age acceleration was the epigenetic clock most consistently associated with 10-year all-cause mortality after multivariable adjustment. In 1,942 NHANES participants, both GrimAge and GrimAge2 age acceleration showed approximately linear positive associations with all-cause mortality. In 1,966 U.S. adults aged 50 and older, each 5-year increase in GrimAge acceleration was associated with a 44% higher all-cause mortality risk.
edges.population: middle-aged and older adults with blood DNA-methylation clock assessment and long-term mortality follow-up
edges.mechanism: GrimAge acceleration summarizes methylation patterns linked to smoking exposure, inflammatory burden, protein surrogates, and biological wear-and-tear. A higher-than-expected GrimAge therefore acts as a condensed signal that multiple mortality-relevant aging pathways are already running faster than chronological age would suggest.
edges.summary: This is one of the cleaner harmful biomarker edges in the batch. Across multiple cohorts, GrimAge acceleration repeatedly outperforms older epigenetic clocks and shows a fairly consistent positive association with all-cause mortality.
edges.caveats: GrimAge is a composite methylation-derived risk marker, not a direct mechanistic cause of death. It is also partly built from smoking- and protein-related surrogates, so its predictive power reflects bundled biology rather than a single aging pathway.

evidence.citation: Cathal McCrory et al 2021 J Gerontol A Biol Sci Med Sci
evidence.notes: GrimAge Outperforms Other Epigenetic Clocks in the Prediction of Age-Related Clinical Phenotypes and All-Cause Mortality.
GrimAge and GrimAge2 Age Acceleration effectively predict mortality risk: a retrospective cohort study.

evidence.notes: Associations between five indicators of epigenetic age acceleration and all-cause and cause-specific mortality among US adults aged 50 years and older.
